principles.title: No Borders Within Borders
principles.summary: Do not place bordered elements inside other bordered elements.
rules: Express hierarchy with background elevation, spacing, typography and subtle section dividers.
A border marks a meaningful boundary, not the existence of an element.
Inputs and rows inside panels are filled surfaces, not outlined boxes.
exceptions: A single outline on a floating overlay (menu, dialog) is allowed.
Checkbox and radio boxes need a visible boundary.

principles.title: Dark Themes Move From Dark to Light
principles.summary: In dark themes each elevated surface is lighter than its parent.
rules: Page is darkest (--s0), main panels --s1, cards and inputs --s2, selected and raised --s3, overlays --s4.
Never make a nested or elevated surface darker than its parent.
Elevation should read without borders.
exceptions: A media lightbox backdrop may be darker than the page so the image dominates.

principles.title: No Arbitrary Left-Border Decoration
principles.summary: Do not use a thicker left border to make an element stand out.
rules: Do not use a thick left border for cards, alerts, active items, info panels, categories or emphasis.
Use fill, type weight or spacing for emphasis instead.
exceptions: The product or user explicitly requires it.
It has an established semantic meaning in that interface (blockquote, diff gutter).

principles.title: Tags Must Be Functional, Not Decorative
principles.summary: Tags exist only when users recognize, filter, group or interact with a category or state.
rules: Default tag: one background color, no border, optional icon, short text.
Never create status tags for information that need not be shown (for example 'Automatically saved').
Do not scatter tags to add visual variety.
exceptions: Label tags that filter or group tasks; a failure state that needs attention.

principles.title: Information Must Earn Its Place
principles.summary: Show the minimum information needed for the current task.
rules: Do not explain familiar concepts because space is available.
Prefer familiar patterns, clear naming, predictable position, progressive disclosure and contextual help over permanent explanation.
A small learning curve beats permanent information overload.
exceptions: Legal or safety text that must be shown.
A one-time first-use hint that can be dismissed.

principles.title: Use as Few Colors as Possible
principles.summary: Color is a limited communication resource.
rules: Rely on neutral surfaces, typography, spacing, shape and hierarchy.
Accent colors communicate meaning, interaction, identity or state.
If removing a color does not reduce comprehension, remove it.
exceptions: Data visualisation, media imagery and market movement legitimately need hues.

principles.title: One Visual Language
principles.summary: All Summa products share one design language.
rules: Share spacing logic, typography, surfaces, interaction states, iconography, corner treatment, controls, menus, navigation patterns and motion.
Theme: matte, restrained, slightly glassy, reusable, consistent.
Applications differ in content and workflow, not in design language.

principles.title: Familiarity Is a Feature
principles.summary: Prefer established interaction conventions.
rules: Do not make users relearn dropdowns, menus, tabs, navigation, search, dialogs, selection, keyboard behavior or editor interactions.
Innovate on workflow, not on controls users already understand.

principles.title: Simplicity Beats Cleverness
principles.summary: Prefer the simpler design when two solve the problem.
rules: Do not add controls, containers, states, visual treatments or terminology without meaningful user value.
Complexity requires justification; simplicity does not.

principles.title: Minimalism Over Prevalence
principles.summary: Do not show every possible action at once.
rules: Prefer contextual and dynamic controls.
Put 'Create' inside the dropdown where it becomes relevant, not beside it.
Show Send before generation and Stop during it, never both.
When a control turns into its opposite (Send to Stop), add an interaction guard against accidental double clicks.
exceptions: Two actions that can genuinely be used at the same moment may both be visible.

principles.title: The Rectangle Rule
principles.summary: Organize information in clean rectangular regions.
rules: Do not use indentation as the primary hierarchy mechanism.
Express hierarchy with typography, text color, weight, size and spacing; body content starts at the same left edge as its heading.
Prefer flat lists, breadcrumbs and a single-level sidebar to indented trees.
exceptions: List marker gutters and table cell padding are not indentation.

principles.title: Dividers Are Secondary Structure
principles.summary: Use subtle horizontal dividers only to support an existing hierarchy.
rules: Prefer spacing first.
Add a divider only when spacing alone leaves two regions ambiguous.
Avoid excessive divider lines.
exceptions: Repeated rows (feed posts, cart lines, review rows) may use one hairline each.

principles.title: No Em Dashes
principles.summary: No em dashes in user-facing interface copy.
rules: Use commas, colons, periods, parentheses or a rewritten sentence.
Applies to headings, descriptions, labels, notifications, empty states and demo content.
Leave empty table cells empty instead of filling them with a dash.

principles.title: No Sidebar Stacking
principles.summary: Never answer sidebar navigation with another full navigation sidebar beside it.
rules: Secondary context: replace the sidebar content with a back chevron, or split the sidebar into upper and lower regions, or use the primary content region for details.
Editors, inspectors, order books and detail panels are content panes and are allowed.
The rule targets redundant navigation structures only.
exceptions: Content panes (watchlist, filters, inspectors) are not navigation sidebars.

principles.title: Monochromatic Selection and Focus
principles.summary: Ordinary selection, hover, focus and active navigation are neutral.
rules: Do not use the emerald accent for focus rings, selected cards, selected nav entries or text input outlines.
Prefer neutral surface changes or neutral outlines.
Keep accessible focus visibility.
Keep semantic colors where they carry meaning (market movement, destructive actions).
Use emerald sparingly: brand, the primary action of a view, meaningful state.
exceptions: Semantic colors for trading movement, KPI deltas and destructive actions.

principles.title: Layout Diversity
principles.summary: No universal left-sidebar/right-content structure.
rules: Choose layout from the task, user expectations and information architecture.
Support dashboards, public sites, feeds, dense data workspaces, catalogs and form-based experiences.
Variety comes from the task, never from novelty; familiarity remains essential.

principles.title: Subtle Focus and Selection
principles.summary: Neutral focus and selection must also be light in visual weight.
rules: Avoid thick, high-contrast or dominant outlines for ordinary input focus, selected content and active controls.
Use 1px to 1.5px neutral rings and quiet fills.
Keyboard focus indicators must still reach at least 3:1 contrast against their surface.
Invisible focus is not tasteful minimalism.
exceptions: Windows high-contrast or forced-colors modes should use system focus styles.

principles.title: Mobile Navigation Breathing Room
principles.summary: Do not compress navigation, headings, filters and actions into dense vertical stacks on mobile.
rules: Leave clear spacing between navigation and primary content.
Do not trade readability and rhythm for more information above the fold.
Scrolling is preferable to compression.
Move secondary controls into a sheet or menu instead of stacking rows.

principles.title: No Washed-Out Destructive Buttons
principles.summary: Destructive buttons are solid and readable, or neutral.
rules: Avoid translucent, low-contrast tinted ghost buttons, especially pale red text on dark red tint.
Use a restrained solid destructive button with readable text, or a neutral treatment when appropriate.
Do not rely on color alone: use a clear verb and an icon where helpful.
exceptions: Destructive menu items use danger-colored text plus an icon and sit last after a separator.

principles.title: No Decorative Placeholder Identity
principles.summary: Do not invent avatars when no meaningful avatar exists.
rules: No circular initials, generated placeholder avatars or artificial profile-picture indicators by default.
Plain names and relevant metadata are often enough.
Introduce an avatar only when identity imagery helps distinguish entities or represents real content.
exceptions: Social platforms where users have real profile images.

principles.title: Remove Before Adding
principles.summary: Meta-principle: when an interface feels unclear, subtract first.
rules: Ask whether something can be removed, merged, relocated, hidden contextually, represented through hierarchy or revealed only when needed before adding a component.

principles.title: Exception Rule
principles.summary: Principles are defaults, not absolute prohibitions.
rules: A principle may be broken only for a concrete usability requirement, when the alternative interacts worse, deliberately, and with an explainable reason.
'Because it looks nicer' is not sufficient justification.
Document every exception.
